content.p: The Finks are an Australian outlaw motorcycle club whose name began as a joke. It comes from the cartoon strip The Wizard of Id, where the line "The King is a fink" is often shouted, and the club's emblem is Bung, the strip's drunk jester. In 2012, the Finks became the first club in Australia to be declared a criminal organisation, according to a former member writing for ABC News. A year later most chapters gave up the name and the colours and became Mongols. Yet the Finks did not disappear: police and courts in Victoria and NSW have been dealing with men they describe as Finks members as recently as late 2025.
content.h2: A cartoon jester and a 1969 start
content.p: One biker-history site says the details of the club's early days are difficult to find, and that most of what has been written covers the years from 2008, when a Perth chapter was formed and tensions with other clubs began to turn violent. The same site, and Mahmood Fazal, who joined the club in Melbourne, both date the club's history back to 1969. Neither source, in the pages used here, says where the club was first formed.

The emblem tells part of the story. The main figure on the patch is Bung, and the colour of his trousers changes according to the member's rank in the club. Fazal described the original patches as "jovial caricatures of the drunk jester", and wrote that the club prided itself on being a distinctly Australian outfit. In 2014, after the Mongols had taken over the Perth chapter, the patch was redesigned. A senior member told the biker site the new figure was much more aggressive than the drunk Bung, a change made partly to send a message to the Mongols.

Fazal, an Afghan-Australian from Melbourne, wrote in 2020 that he had been drawn to the Finks by a longing to belong. He said he was asked to "show face" at the club, which felt to him like "a thuggish knighthood". Passing through the guarded gates, he recalled, the tension was "turbulent and lawless". The first year was spent hanging around social events before he was asked to a meeting night and then to serve as a nominee.

Nominees, he wrote, were told in short sentences what to expect: "If you're here to make money, piss off. If you have a girlfriend she's going to leave you. The only holidays you'll be taking are to jail." The patch was the thing that bound the brotherhood. He recalled that a nominee who drunkenly left his vest in a back room had his face stomped and booted, and that his chapter president told him the colours were "easy to get, but hard to keep". Everyone had day jobs, he said, and the club motto was "whatever, whenever".

This is one man's account, written after he had left, and he does not claim to speak for every member. It is useful for what it shows of the club's own rules and the pull of the patch, not as a record of what the club did.

The One Percenter Bikers site says the Perth chapter was founded in 2008 by Troy Mercanti, who had previously been in the Coffin Cheaters, and Frank Condo, who had been in the South Australian chapter. Interstate members joined at first but dropped off until the Perth membership could, the site says, be counted on one hand. The new chapter caused tension with the Coffin Cheaters.

That tension reached a public setting on the weekend of 2 and 3 October 2010 at the Perth Motorplex, at a Harley Street drag-racing event. The site says it was claimed that one club member spat on a rival. The site says one Finks member, David Marrapodi, was shot in the leg, another lost three fingers, and a third man suffered serious head wounds. Afterwards, it says, five Finks members were imprisoned for two years in November 2010 for contempt, after refusing to cooperate with a joint police and Corruption and Crime Commission investigation.

The Perth clubhouse also came under legal pressure. The site reports that Mercanti's partner, Tammy Kingdon, was convicted of stealing and property laundering in 2010. It says the money came from a fund the Coffin Cheaters had set up for the daughters of a murdered member, that it paid for the clubhouse, and that the building was then frozen under proceeds-of-crime law. These are claims from a single enthusiast site; the primary court reports were not available for this account.

The most fully documented court case from the Perth period involved no club dispute at all. In January 2012 Kingdon went to police with allegations of abuse by Mercanti. WAtoday reported in March 2013 that Mercanti, then 45, had pleaded not guilty to five charges, including inflicting grievous bodily harm, but changed his pleas to guilty on all but one charge two weeks into his trial, after Kingdon had endured more than three days of cross-examination. The court heard that the abuse began in 1997, when he punched her in the face at a Bunbury hotel and fractured her eye, and that other beatings left her with fractured ribs and black eyes. His own mother gave evidence against him, testifying that she saw him punch Kingdon at a Christmas lunch in 2006.

Judge Simon Stone of the District Court of Western Australia sentenced Mercanti to six years and ten months, backdated to his arrest on 3 March 2012, and said he posed "a significant risk to her life and safety". The judge and prosecutor both stressed that the sentence was not a punishment for belonging to a motorcycle club. "He's to be punished as a criminal offender who's enacted a series of cowardly, brutal and unprovoked assaults against a defenceless woman, smaller than himself," the judge said. WAtoday gave the abuse as 16 years; the biker site gave the period as 15 years.

In 2012 the Finks were declared a criminal organisation, the first club in Australia to be so declared, according to Fazal's account. He wrote that members lost jobs, some moved interstate for work, and most of the Queensland chapter sold their bikes to fund a High Court challenge to the legislation. The following year Queensland introduced the Vicious Lawless Association Disestablishment (VLAD) Act, intended, in the quoted phrase, to "come down harshly on outlaw motorcycle gangs and their members".

Facing that pressure, each chapter voted on whether to patch over to the Mongols, an international club with similar black and white colours. Fazal called it "a vote for survival" and said some members felt they were turning their backs on the club's Australian roots. The biker site says the Perth chapter and most other Australian chapters were patched over in late 2013.

A Queensland shooting had already drawn attention. The biker site records that Mark James Graham, a Finks member, was charged on 28 April 2012 with attempting to murder a rival Bandidos member in a shopping-centre shooting at Robina, and that he received a 12-year prison term in November 2014. The same site says the Finks were also named in 2001 as a target of Operation Avatar, a South Australian police task force aimed at one-percenter clubs.

Brent Reker, described as a Finks boss in the Melbourne newspaper report on the coroner's hearing, was 35 and on remand for violent drug and weapon offences when he was found unconscious in his cell at Ravenhall prison on 12 December 2019. Counsel assisting the coroner told a hearing in March 2023 that he had been transferred in November 2019 from another prison to a specialist mental health unit after earlier attempts to take his own life. About three weeks later staff worried he was influencing other prisoners, and a case conference decided he should be moved. A psychiatrist was meant to speak to him first but the clinician had already left the unit. He was told of the move about 2.30 pm; a psychiatrist reached his new cell about 3.30 pm, the door was blocked by a mattress, and he was found at 3.38 pm. Coroner Paul Lawrie was examining the lead-up to the move and whether it contributed to his taking his own life. The pages used here do not give a finding.

In April 2024 a judge of the Victorian County Court sentenced a high-ranking member, Paul Robert "Romeo" Draper, 40, after he pleaded guilty to robbery, assault, extortion with a threat to inflict injury, theft of a number plate and possession of steroids. The court heard that in July 2021 Draper and two other full-patch members went to the Doncaster home of a Finks treasurer who was deciding whether to leave, and that Draper demanded his $60,000 Harley-Davidson. Draper assaulted the man, and another member warned him not to call police. A week later, at Draper's home, he was told he would have to pay $15,000 and forfeit the bike to leave; he signed over the bike, was beaten, and over several weeks transferred $11,500. Echo Taskforce police raided homes and the Cranbourne West clubhouse in October. Judge Sarah Leighfield called Draper the "principal" offender and imposed seven months' jail followed by a 21-month community corrections order, limiting a non-association condition to the first nine months. Three other members had earlier received community corrections orders.
content.h2: Arson, tobacco and a Hunter weekend
content.p: On 12 January 2024 police arrested five people over a run of arson attacks on tobacco shops and a cafe around Melbourne. Three of the men, aged 41, 30 and 32, were described as believed to be patched Finks members; they were charged with arson counts, with one also charged with aggravated carjacking, and remanded. A fourth man, 37, was charged with five arson counts, and a 17-year-old was interviewed and released pending inquiries. Police said they believed syndicates, made up of Middle Eastern organised crime groups and outlaw motorcycle gangs, were competing over illicit tobacco and using local youths to carry out the offending. These are allegations at the time of arrest; the pages used do not report the outcomes.

In NSW, five Sydney men were charged in March 2025 over an attempted break-in at a Belmont North home on 23 February, where a 38-year-old man was shot in the stomach. Police alleged several of them were high-ranking Finks members, and four of the men were refused bail. In November 2025 the Raptor Squad North raided seven properties across Lake Macquarie, Cessnock and Maitland after two weekends of pub brawls at Merewether and Shoal Bay, arresting eight alleged members and associates and a partner of one. Police said they had seized firearms, drugs and cash. Of those charged, four were refused bail by police; the others were released on bail. All were accused only and the outcomes were not available.
